claim: The GrabFP system is a collection of four nanobody-based GFP-traps that localize to defined positions along the apical-basal axis.
source: Here, we present the GrabFP system, a collection of four nanobody-based GFP-traps that localize to defined positions along the apical-basal axis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the system.

claim: The localization preference of the GrabFP traps can impose a novel localization on GFP-tagged target proteins and results in their controlled mislocalization.
source: We show that the localization preference of the GrabFP traps can impose a novel localization on GFP-tagged target proteins and results in their controlled mislocalization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: The GrabFP system was used to mislocalize transmembrane and cytoplasmic GFP fusion proteins in the Drosophila wing disc epithelium.
source: These new tools were used to mislocalize transmembrane and cytoplasmic GFP fusion proteins in the Drosophila wing disc epithelium and to investigate the effect of protein mislocalization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an application of the system.

claim: The Dpp gradient forming in the lateral plane of the Drosophila wing disc epithelium is essential for patterning of the wing imaginal disc.
source: Furthermore, we used the GrabFP system as a tool to study the extracellular dispersal of the Decapentaplegic (Dpp) protein and show that the Dpp gradient forming in the lateral plane of the Drosophila wing disc epithelium is essential for patterning of the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding from using the GrabFP system.

claim: vhhGFP4 is a nanobody that specifically recognizes GFP.
source: One class of widely applied protein binders are the so-called nanobodies, which are derived from single chain antibodies found in members of the Camelid family. A nanobody specifically recognizing GFP (vhhGFP4, Saerens et al., 2005) has been extensively used for cell and developmental biology applications.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Saerens et al., 2005.

claim: vhhGFP4 functions in the intracellular environment and can be fused to other proteins without losing its activity and specificity in vivo.
source: Importantly, vhhGFP4 functions in the intracellular environment and can be fused to other proteins without losing its activity and specificity in vivo (Rothbauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Rothbauer et al., 2008.

claim: vhhGFP4 has been functionalized by fusing it to different protein domains to visualize, relocalize, and degrade GFP-tagged proteins of interest.
source: As a consequence, vhhGFP4 has been functionalized by fusing it to different protein domains in order to visualize (Rothbauer et al., 2006), relocalize (Berry et al., 2016) and degrade (Caussinus et al., 2012; Shin et al., 2015) GFP-tagged proteins of interest.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Morphotrap consists of a fusion protein between vhhGFP4 and the mouse CD8 transmembrane protein, designed such that the nanobody is presented extracellularly along the surface of cells.
source: Morphotrap consists of a fusion protein between vhhGFP4 and the mouse CD8 transmembrane protein, designed such that the nanobody is presented extracellularly along the surface of cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the morphotrap construct.

claim: Morphotrap proved to be a powerful tool to modify and study secretion and extracellular dispersal of eGFP-Dpp in the Drosophila wing disc tissue.
source: In combination with a GFP-tagged version of the Decapentaplegic (eGFP-Dpp) morphogen, morphotrap proved to be a powerful tool to modify and study secretion and extracellular dispersal of eGFP-Dpp in the Drosophila wing disc tissue (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Harmansa et al., 2015.

claim: The GrabFP toolbox consists of morphotrap and five novel synthetic GFP-traps.
source: Here, we introduce the GrabFP (grab Green Fluorescent Protein) toolbox, consisting of morphotrap and five novel synthetic GFP-traps that either localize to both the apical and basolateral compartment (morphotrap) or preferentially to one compartment: apical (GrabFP-A) or basolateral (GrabFP-B, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the composition of the GrabFP system.

claim: Morphotrap localizes to both the apical and basolateral compartment.
source: Here, we introduce the GrabFP (grab Green Fluorescent Protein) toolbox, consisting of morphotrap and five novel synthetic GFP-traps that either localize to both the apical and basolateral compartment (morphotrap) or preferentially to one compartment: apical (GrabFP-A) or basolateral (GrabFP-B, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: GrabFP-A localizes preferentially to the apical compartment.
source: Here, we introduce the GrabFP (grab Green Fluorescent Protein) toolbox, consisting of morphotrap and five novel synthetic GFP-traps that either localize to both the apical and basolateral compartment (morphotrap) or preferentially to one compartment: apical (GrabFP-A) or basolateral (GrabFP-B, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GrabFP-B localizes preferentially to the basolateral compartment.
source: Here, we introduce the GrabFP (grab Green Fluorescent Protein) toolbox, consisting of morphotrap and five novel synthetic GFP-traps that either localize to both the apical and basolateral compartment (morphotrap) or preferentially to one compartment: apical (GrabFP-A) or basolateral (GrabFP-B, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: For each of the three localizations (apical/basolateral, apical, basolateral), two versions were constructed in which the vhhGFP4 domain either faces the extracellular space (GrabFPExt) or the intracellular milieu (GrabFPInt).
source: For each of these three localizations, two versions were constructed in which the vhhGFP4 domain either faces the extracellular space (GrabFPExt) or the intracellular milieu (GrabFPInt).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the design of the GrabFP system.

claim: The GrabFP system can be used to interfere with target proteins in the extracellular and the intracellular space.
source: Consequently, the GrabFP system can be used to interfere with target proteins in the extracellular and the intracellular space (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of the design.

claim: The Drosophila wing imaginal disc epithelium is a well-characterized model system to study epithelial polarity.
source: To test the localization and function of the GrabFP system, we made use of the Drosophila wing imaginal disc epithelium, a well-characterized model system to study epithelial polarity (Tepass, 2012; Flores-Benitez and Knust, 2016) and dispersal of extracellular signaling proteins, for example morphogens (Thérond, 2012; Gradilla and Guerrero, 2013; Akiyama and Gibson, 2015; Langton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Tepass, 2012 and Flores-Benitez and Knust, 2016.

claim: The Drosophila wing imaginal disc epithelium is a well-characterized model system to study dispersal of extracellular signaling proteins, for example morphogens.
source: To test the localization and function of the GrabFP system, we made use of the Drosophila wing imaginal disc epithelium, a well-characterized model system to study epithelial polarity (Tepass, 2012; Flores-Benitez and Knust, 2016) and dispersal of extracellular signaling proteins, for example morphogens (Thérond, 2012; Gradilla and Guerrero, 2013; Akiyama and Gibson, 2015; Langton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The wing imaginal disc consists of two contiguous, monolayered epithelial sheets, the pseudo stratified disc proper (DP) epithelium and the squamous peripodial epithelium (PPE).
source: The wing imaginal disc consists of two contiguous, monolayered epithelial sheets, the pseudo stratified disc proper (DP) epithelium and the squamous peripodial epithelium (PPE; see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The apical surface of both the DP and the PPE is facing a luminal cavity formed between them.
source: The apical surface of both, the DP and the PPE, is facing a luminal cavity formed between them.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the wing disc structure.

claim: Visualization of the junctions via the localization of the septate junction component Discs-large (Dlg) was used to mark the border separating the apical and basolateral compartment in DP cells.
source: Visualization of the junctions via the localization of the septate junction component Discs-large (Dlg, see Materials and methods) was used to mark the border separating the apical and basolateral compartment in DP cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the methodology.

claim: Morphotrap, based on the mouse CD8 protein scaffold, localizes to both the apical and the basolateral domains.
source: Morphotrap, based on the mouse CD8 protein scaffold, was shown to localize to both the apical and the basolateral domains (see Figure 1C and Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1C and citation to Harmansa et al., 2015.

claim: MorphotrapInt, in which the nanobody faces the cytosol, localizes to the apical and basolateral compartments.
source: The morphotrapInt construct, in which the nanobody faces the cytosol, also localizes to the apical and basolateral compartments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GrabFP-A is based on the transcript 48 (T48) protein.
source: In order to generate an apically anchored trap (GrabFP-A), we made use of the transcript 48 (T48) protein (Kölsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Kölsch et al., 2007.

claim: A fusion protein between the GFP-nanobody, T48, and mCherry showed only mild apical enrichment.
source: However, since a fusion protein between the GFP-nanobody, T48, and mCherry showed only mild apical enrichment (not shown), we additionally attached the minimal localization domain of Bazooka (Krahn et al., 2010) to the C-terminus of the fusion protein (see Figure 1A and Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the design of GrabFP-A.

claim: The minimal localization domain of Bazooka was attached to the C-terminus of the GrabFP-A fusion protein to enhance apical localization.
source: However, since a fusion protein between the GFP-nanobody, T48, and mCherry showed only mild apical enrichment (not shown), we additionally attached the minimal localization domain of Bazooka (Krahn et al., 2010) to the C-terminus of the fusion protein (see Figure 1A and Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Krahn et al., 2010.

claim: Expression in DP cells of both versions of GrabFP-A, GrabFP-AExt and GrabFP-AInt, resulted in strong enrichment in the apical compartment.
source: Expression in DP cells of both versions of GrabFP-A, GrabFP-AExt and GrabFP-AInt, resulted in strong enrichment in the apical compartment, while only minor amounts of GrabFP-AExt or GrabFP-AInt were observed along the basolateral domain (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only minor amounts of GrabFP-AExt or GrabFP-AInt were observed along the basolateral domain.
source: Expression in DP cells of both versions of GrabFP-A, GrabFP-AExt and GrabFP-AInt, resulted in strong enrichment in the apical compartment, while only minor amounts of GrabFP-AExt or GrabFP-AInt were observed along the basolateral domain (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GrabFP-B is based on the Nrv1 protein scaffold.
source: Our basolaterally anchored GFP-trap GrabFP-B is based on the Nrv1 protein scaffold (Figure 1A, Sun and Salvaterra, 1995; Xu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Sun and Salvaterra, 1995 and Xu et al., 1999.

claim: Nrv1 localizes to the basolateral compartment of the wing disc, even when overexpressed.
source: Nrv1 localizes to the basolateral compartment of the wing disc, even when overexpressed (Genova and Fehon, 2003; Paul et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Genova and Fehon, 2003 and Paul et al., 2007.

claim: In DP cells, GrabFP-BExt and GrabFP-BInt exclusively localized to the basolateral compartment with no detectable signal along the apical compartment.
source: In DP cells, GrabFP-BExt and GrabFP-BInt exclusively localized to the basolateral compartment with no detectable signal along the apical compartment (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of the GrabFP constructs in the wing imaginal disc yielded viable and fertile adults with proper wing blade size.
source: Expression of the GrabFP constructs in the wing imaginal disc yielded viable and fertile adults with proper wing blade size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the GrabFP system is inert in the absence of GFP and can be used as a tool to study protein function along the A-B axis in the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The GrabFP system is inert in the absence of GFP.
source: Expression of the GrabFP constructs in the wing imaginal disc yielded viable and fertile adults with proper wing blade size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the GrabFP system is inert in the absence of GFP and can be used as a tool to study protein function along the A-B axis in the wing imaginal disc.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the observation that expression does not affect viability or wing size.

claim: The interaction between localized GFP-traps and a GFP-tagged target protein can result in defined mislocalization of the target protein.
source: We wanted to test whether the interaction between our localized GFP-traps and a GFP-tagged target protein, transmembrane or cytosolic, can result in defined mislocalization of the target protein.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis that was tested in the study.

claim: A total of 15 GFP/YFP-tagged proteins were analyzed for changes in distribution along the A-B axis, of which 11 were transmembrane/membrane-anchored and four were cytoplasmic proteins.
source: We analysed and measured the changes in distribution along the A-B axis of a total of 15 GFP/YFP-tagged proteins, of which 11 were transmembrane/membrane-anchored and four were cytoplasmic proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the scope of the analysis.

claim: Binding of nanobodies can interfere with the fluorescent properties of GFP.
source: However, it is known that the binding of nanobodies can interfere with the fluorescent properties of GFP (Kirchhofer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Kirchhofer et al., 2010.

claim: Binding of vhhGFP4 to eGFP results in a 1.47-fold increase in eGFP fluorescence in vitro.
source: Indeed, we observed that binding of vhhGFP4 to eGFP modulated the fluorescent properties of eGFP and resulted in a 1.47-fold increase in eGFP fluorescence in vitro (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of either GrabFP-AExt or GrabFP-BExt caused significant changes in the distribution of all eight transmembrane proteins tested.
source: Expression of either GrabFP-AExt (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) or GrabFP-BExt (Figure 2D,E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D) caused significant changes in the distribution of all eight proteins tested.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to multiple figures.

claim: GrabFP-AExt efficiently induced mislocalization of target proteins.
source: Generally, GrabFP-AExt efficiently induced mislocalization of target proteins (i.e. the gain of a novel apical fraction in proteins excluded from the apical compartment, as seen for NrxIV-YFP, Figure 2B) and stabilization of an existing apical fraction (as seen for Dlp-YFP, Dally-YFP, PMCA-YFP, Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to specific examples in figures.

claim: GrabFP-AExt expression did not result in efficient depletion of the basolateral protein fraction.
source: However, GrabFP-AExt expression did not result in efficient depletion of the basolateral protein fraction (see plots Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 2B–C.

claim: GrabFP-AExt was partially mislocalized by the interaction with polarized target proteins and showed enhanced localization to the basolateral compartment.
source: This might be due to the fact that GrabFP-AExt itself was partially mislocalized by the interaction with polarized target proteins and showed enhanced localization to the basolateral compartment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an explanation for the observation, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: GrabFP-BExt displayed a strong potential in depleting apical target-protein fractions.
source: In contrast, GrabFP-BExt displayed a strong potential in depleting apical target-protein fractions (Figure 2D–F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to multiple figures.

claim: GrabFP-BExt significantly reduced the apical pool and increased the basolateral fraction of Dally-YFP, Notch-YFP, Fra-YFP, Crb-GFP and Ed-YFP.
source: In particular, GrabFP-BExt significantly reduced the apical pool and increased the basolateral fraction of Dally-YFP, Notch-YFP, Fra-YFP, Crb-GFP and Ed-YFP.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the effects of GrabFP-BExt on specific proteins.

claim: GrabFP-BExt was resistant to mislocalization induced by target protein-interaction.
source: Furthermore, GrabFP-BExt was resistant to mislocalization induced by target protein-interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Expression of the GrabFP constructs altered the subcellular localization along the apical-basal axis of the 15 different GFP-tagged cytosolic or transmembrane proteins tested.
source: Recently, it was reported that tethering of nanobodies to specific cellular compartments can result in protein relocalization (Berry et al., 2016). In line with these observations, expression of the GrabFP constructs altered the subcellular localization along the apical-basal axis of the 15 different GFP-tagged cytosolic or transmembrane proteins we tested.
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Berry et al., 2016.

claim: All the different components of the GrabFP system induced drastic mislocalization of target proteins, causing the gain of a novel subcellular fraction, which was minor or absent in wild-type conditions.
source: All the different components of the GrabFP system induced drastic mislocalization of target proteins, causing the gain of a novel subcellular fraction, which was minor or absent in wild-type conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the results summarizing the effects of the GrabFP system.

claim: The GrabFP system significantly depleted the wild-type subcellular fractions of two-thirds of the tested target proteins.
source: In addition, the GrabFP system significantly depleted the wild-type subcellular fractions of two-thirds of the tested target proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results summarizing the effects of the GrabFP system.

claim: Notch signaling is required for cell-cell communication and differentiation during development.
source: Notch signaling is required for cell-cell communication and differentiation during development (Guruharsha et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Guruharsha et al., 2012.

claim: The apical localization of Notch is conserved in different tissues and organisms.
source: The apical localization of Notch is conserved in different tissues and organisms, suggesting that it is crucial for Notch function (Fehon et al., 1991; Ohata et al., 2011; Hatakeyama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Notch apical localization might be necessary to allow interaction with its ligand Delta, which also localizes to the apical cell surface.
source: In particular, Notch apical localization might be necessary to allow interaction with its ligand Delta, which also localizes to the apical cell surface (Sasaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation with citation to Sasaki et al., 2007.

claim: The GrabFP components were in some cases themselves mislocalized due to interaction with target proteins.
source: In line with observations made by Berry et al. (Schornack et al., 2009; Berry et al., 2016), the GrabFP components were in some cases themselves mislocalized due to interaction with target proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to Schornack et al., 2009 and Berry et al., 2016.

claim: GrabFP-AExt and GrabFP-BInt were less efficient in causing target protein mislocalization, presumably as a consequence of being themselves mislocalized.
source: This was particularly relevant for GrabFP-AExt and GrabFP-BInt (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H), which were, presumably as a consequence, less efficient in causing target protein mislocalization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to figures.

claim: Large collections of GFP-tagged protein are available in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Conveniently, large collections of GFP-tagged protein are available in Drosophila melanogaster (Lowe et al., 2014; Lye et al., 2014; Nagarkar-Jaiswal et al., 2015; Sarov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The GrabFP system can be induced in a tissue-specific and temporally controlled manner.
source: Moreover, the GrabFP system can be induced in a tissue-specific and temporally controlled manner and thus represents a versatile tool to study the effect of forced protein mislocalization and protein function in specific subcellular compartments in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion describing the advantages of the system.

claim: Tissue-specific degradation of Sqh combined with laser ablation studies have shown that amnioserosa cell constriction but not actin cable tension in the adjacent dorsal ectodermal cells autonomously drives dorsal closure.
source: Tissue-specific degradation of Sqh (which leads to a failure to contract actomyosin networks) combined with laser ablation studies have now shown that amnioserosa cell constriction but not actin cable tension in the adjacent dorsal ectodermal cells autonomously drives dorsal closure (Pasakarnis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Pasakarnis et al., 2016.

claim: Morphotrap was used to show that spreading of eGFP-Dpp is required for wing pouch patterning and for medial growth, while it is dispensable for lateral wing disc growth.
source: We have previously used morphotrap to show that spreading of eGFP-Dpp is required for wing pouch patterning and for medial growth, while it is dispensable for lateral wing disc growth (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Harmansa et al., 2015.

claim: The vast majority of the eGFP-Dpp pool can be immobilized on the basolateral side of disc cells, indicating that Dpp spreads in the basolateral intercellular space.
source: We find that the vast majority of the eGFP-Dpp pool can be immobilized on the basolateral side of disc cells, indicating that Dpp spreads in the basolateral intercellular space.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a finding from the study.

claim: Functional interference with Dpp spreading in the basolateral compartment only (GrabFP-BExt) suggests that the patterning function of the Dpp gradient is brought about to a large extend by Dpp spreading in the lateral plane of the wing disc epithelium.
source: In line with this, functional interference with Dpp spreading in the basolateral compartment only (GrabFP-BExt) suggests that the patterning function of the Dpp gradient is brought about to a large extend by Dpp spreading in the lateral plane of the wing disc epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Growth control is influenced by Dpp dispersing in both the lateral and in the basal planes.
source: Growth control, in contrast, is influenced by Dpp dispersing in both the lateral and in the basal planes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Restricting basolateral Dpp dispersal (using GrabFP-BExt) strongly impairs pattern and size.
source: These results are based on the findings that restricting basolateral Dpp dispersal (using GrabFP-BExt) strongly impairs pattern and size while immobilizing eGFP-Dpp in the BL (using GrabFP-ECM) only impairs the size of the Drosophila wing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: Immobilizing eGFP-Dpp in the BL (using GrabFP-ECM) only impairs the size of the Drosophila wing.
source: These results are based on the findings that restricting basolateral Dpp dispersal (using GrabFP-BExt) strongly impairs pattern and size while immobilizing eGFP-Dpp in the BL (using GrabFP-ECM) only impairs the size of the Drosophila wing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: Several mechanisms for morphogen gradient formation have been suggested, operating in different extracellular environments.
source: Dpp gradient formation in the Drosophila wing disc remains a paradigm to study morphogen dispersal and several mechanisms for morphogen gradient formation have been suggested, operating in different extracellular environments (for a recent review see [Akiyama and Gibson, 2015]).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Akiyama and Gibson, 2015.

claim: Proposed mechanisms for morphogen gradient formation include free extracellular diffusion in the wing disc lumen.
source: These proposed mechanisms include free extracellular diffusion in the wing disc lumen (Zhou et al., 2012), restricted extracellular diffusion in the lateral plane of the epithelium (Belenkaya et al., 2004; Akiyama et al., 2008; Schwank et al., 2011), and active transport by actin-based filopodial extensions called cytonemes along the apical surface of DP cells (Hsiung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: Proposed mechanisms for morphogen gradient formation include restricted extracellular diffusion in the lateral plane of the epithelium.
source: These proposed mechanisms include free extracellular diffusion in the wing disc lumen (Zhou et al., 2012), restricted extracellular diffusion in the lateral plane of the epithelium (Belenkaya et al., 2004; Akiyama et al., 2008; Schwank et al., 2011), and active transport by actin-based filopodial extensions called cytonemes along the apical surface of DP cells (Hsiung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Proposed mechanisms for morphogen gradient formation include active transport by actin-based filopodial extensions called cytonemes along the apical surface of DP cells.
source: These proposed mechanisms include free extracellular diffusion in the wing disc lumen (Zhou et al., 2012), restricted extracellular diffusion in the lateral plane of the epithelium (Belenkaya et al., 2004; Akiyama et al., 2008; Schwank et al., 2011), and active transport by actin-based filopodial extensions called cytonemes along the apical surface of DP cells (Hsiung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Hsiung et al., 2005.

claim: The formation of the functional Dpp gradient in the lateral compartment is compatible with a restricted extracellular diffusion mechanism.
source: While the formation of the functional Dpp gradient in the lateral compartment is compatible with a restricted extracellular diffusion mechanism, it is not as easily compatible with the formation of a functional Dpp gradient via free diffusion in the lumen or with a key role of apical cytonemes in Dpp readout.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The formation of the functional Dpp gradient in the lateral compartment is not as easily compatible with the formation of a functional Dpp gradient via free diffusion in the lumen.
source: While the formation of the functional Dpp gradient in the lateral compartment is compatible with a restricted extracellular diffusion mechanism, it is not as easily compatible with the formation of a functional Dpp gradient via free diffusion in the lumen or with a key role of apical cytonemes in Dpp readout.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The formation of the functional Dpp gradient in the lateral compartment is not as easily compatible with a key role of apical cytonemes in Dpp readout.
source: While the formation of the functional Dpp gradient in the lateral compartment is compatible with a restricted extracellular diffusion mechanism, it is not as easily compatible with the formation of a functional Dpp gradient via free diffusion in the lumen or with a key role of apical cytonemes in Dpp readout.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Several studies highlighted that Dpp morphogen receptors and interaction partners found along the extracellular surface of target cells crucially influence morphogen gradient shape.
source: In line with Dpp gradient formation via restricted extracellular diffusion, several studies highlighted that Dpp morphogen receptors (Lecuit et al., 1996; Lecuit and Cohen, 1998; Lander et al., 2002; Crickmore and Mann, 2006) and interaction partners (e.g. Dally, Belenkaya et al., 2004, Akiyama et al., 2008) found along the extracellular surface of target cells crucially influence morphogen gradient shape.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to multiple studies.

claim: GrabFP-BInt efficiently depleted the apical fraction of Fat-GFP and induced strong enrichment of its basolateral fraction.
source: GrabFP-BInt efficiently depleted the apical fraction of Fat-GFP and induced strong enrichment of its basolateral fraction (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: GrabFP-BInt was less efficient in mislocalizing and depleting the apical fraction of the cytoplasmic proteins αCat-GFP and Arm-GFP.
source: In contrast, GrabFP-BInt was less efficient in mislocalizing and depleting the apical fraction of the cytoplasmic proteins αCat-GFP and Arm-GFP (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figures.

claim: GrabFP-BInt showed a higher tendency to be mislocalized when co-expressed with αCat-GFP and Arm-GFP.
source: Concomitantly, GrabFP-BInt showed a higher tendency to be mislocalized when co-expressed with these two cytosolic targets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GrabFP-AInt efficiently mislocalized target proteins by decreasing their basolateral concentration and increasing their apical fraction.
source: In contrast, GrabFP-AInt efficiently mislocalized target proteins by decreasing their basolateral concentration and increasing their apical fraction.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the effects of GrabFP-AInt.

claim: All proteins tested in combination with GrabFP-AInt had a strong bias toward the basolateral side in wild-type conditions and acquired a strong apical fraction when co-expressed with GrabFP-AInt.
source: Notably, all proteins tested in combination with GrabFP-AInt had a strong bias toward the basolateral side in wild-type conditions and acquired a strong apical fraction when co-expressed with GrabFP-AInt (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 3D–F.

claim: GrabFP-AInt showed to be resistant to mislocalization induced by target protein interaction.
source: Furthermore, GrabFP-AInt showed to be resistant to mislocalization induced by target protein interaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sqh-GFP is a cytosolic protein that localizes to the subapical cortex in wing disc cells.
source: Drosophila Sqh is crucial for morphogenesis and control of epithelial cell shape (Young et al., 1993; Kiehart et al., 2000). Sqh-GFP is a cytosolic protein that localizes to the subapical cortex in wing disc cells (Figure 4A) and is required for maintaining the elongated shape of DP cells (Widmann and Dahmann, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 4A and citations.

claim: Sqh is required for maintaining the elongated shape of DP cells.
source: Drosophila Sqh is crucial for morphogenesis and control of epithelial cell shape (Young et al., 1993; Kiehart et al., 2000). Sqh-GFP is a cytosolic protein that localizes to the subapical cortex in wing disc cells (Figure 4A) and is required for maintaining the elongated shape of DP cells (Widmann and Dahmann, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Widmann and Dahmann, 2009.

claim: Expression of GrabFP-BInt in sqhSqh-GFP female flies that are heterozygous for sqhAX4 resulted in increased Sqh-GFP levels in the basolateral domain and concomitant reduction in the basal cell surface.
source: Expression of GrabFP-BInt in sqhSqh-GFP female flies that are heterozygous for sqhAX4 (and hence, carry one wild-type and one GFP-tagged copy of Sqh) resulted in increased Sqh-GFP levels in the basolateral domain and concomitant reduction in the basal cell surface (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 4B–C.

claim: In sqhSqh-GFP male flies, which are hemizygous for sqhAX4, Sqh-GFP mislocalization with GrabFP-BInt caused a strong constriction of the basolateral domain accompanied by a significant expansion of the apical cell surface.
source: In sqhSqh-GFP male flies, which are hemizygous for sqhAX4 (and in which Sqh-GFP represents the only source of Sqh protein), Sqh-GFP mislocalization with GrabFP-BInt caused an even more drastic alteration of cell shape (Figure 4D) visible as a strong constriction of the basolateral domain accompanied by a significant expansion of the apical cell surface (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 4D, F–G.

claim: The cell shape alteration caused by Sqh-GFP mislocalization could be explained by loss of apical tension (due to the reduction of apical Sqh-GFP) and increased basolateral tension (due to mislocalized Sqh-GFP).
source: This behavior could be explained by loss of apical tension (due to the reduction of apical Sqh-GFP) and increased basolateral tension (due to mislocalized Sqh-GFP) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an explanation for the observed phenotype, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: GrabFP-BInt altered the localization of Sqh-GFP, presumably causing significant alterations in the force distribution along the cortex of DP cells.
source: In conclusion, GrabFP-BInt altered the localization of Sqh-GFP, presumably causing significant alterations in the force distribution along the cortex of DP cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the Sqh-GFP experiments.

claim: In the developing wing imaginal disc, Dpp is expressed and secreted from a central stripe of anterior cells adjacent to the anterior/posterior (A/P) compartment boundary from where it forms a concentration gradient into the surrounding target tissue.
source: In the developing wing imaginal disc, Dpp is expressed and secreted from a central stripe of anterior cells adjacent to the anterior/posterior (A/P) compartment boundary from where it forms a concentration gradient into the surrounding target tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing Dpp expression and gradient formation.

claim: The Dpp gradient in the wing disc has been visualized by using different GFP-Dpp fusion proteins.
source: The Dpp gradient in the wing disc has been visualized by using different GFP-Dpp fusion proteins (Entchev et al., 2000; Teleman and Cohen, 2000) and by antibody staining against endogenous Dpp protein (Gibson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dpp was observed in the lateral plane of the wing disc epithelial cells.
source: Dpp was observed in the lateral plane of the wing disc epithelial cells (Teleman and Cohen, 2000) as well as apically in the wing disc lumen (Entchev et al., 2000; Gibson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Teleman and Cohen, 2000.

claim: Dpp was observed apically in the wing disc lumen.
source: Dpp was observed in the lateral plane of the wing disc epithelial cells (Teleman and Cohen, 2000) as well as apically in the wing disc lumen (Entchev et al., 2000; Gibson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Entchev et al., 2000 and Gibson et al., 2002.

claim: The results of different studies on Dpp localization were not entirely consistent and hence the routes of Dpp dispersal remain controversial.
source: However, the results of these different studies were not entirely consistent and hence the routes of Dpp dispersal remain controversial.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the controversy in the field.

claim: An eGFP-Dpp fusion protein was shown to rescue the dpp mutant phenotype.
source: To investigate the localization of Dpp in the wing disc, we used an eGFP-Dpp fusion protein that was shown to rescue the dpp mutant phenotype (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Harmansa et al., 2015.

claim: When eGFP-Dpp is expressed in its endogenous expression domain using the LexA/LOP binary expression system, it forms a wide concentration gradient into the target tissue.
source: When eGFP-Dpp is expressed in its endogenous expression domain using the LexA/LOP binary expression system (dpp::LG, Yagi et al., 2010), it forms a wide concentration gradient into the target tissue (Figure 5A and [Harmansa et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 5A and citations.

claim: eGFP-Dpp localized prominently to dotted structures along the lateral region of the DP.
source: Optical cross-sections revealed that eGFP-Dpp localized prominently to dotted structures along the lateral region of the DP (Figure 5B, arrowheads), which were suggested to represent endocytic vesicles (Teleman and Cohen, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 5B and citation to Teleman and Cohen, 2000.

claim: eGFP-Dpp signal was not detected within the luminal space using fluorescence microscopy.
source: We did not detect eGFP-Dpp signal within the luminal space (Figure 5B, magnification).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Using fluorescence microscopy, Dpp is prominently detected within the lateral plane of the DP epithelium.
source: These results suggest that, using fluorescence microscopy, Dpp is prominently detected within the lateral plane of the DP epithelium.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: Morphotrap was reported to immobilize and accumulate eGFP-Dpp on the cell surface.
source: Morphotrap was reported to immobilize and accumulate eGFP-Dpp on the cell surface (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Harmansa et al., 2015.

claim: High amounts of immobilized eGFP-Dpp were observed on the proximal surface of morphotrap clones situated in the target tissue.
source: When we expressed eGFP-Dpp in its central stripe source (using dpp::LG) and morphotrap in clones (Figure 5C), we observed high amounts of immobilized eGFP-Dpp on the proximal surface (the one facing the source of Dpp) of morphotrap clones situated in the target tissue (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 5D–E.

claim: Low amounts of eGFP-Dpp accumulated on the apical surface of morphotrap clones.
source: Subapical projections (Figure 5D) as well as optical cross sections (Figure 5E') showed that low amounts of eGFP-Dpp accumulated on the apical surface of morphotrap clones.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 5D and 5E'.

claim: The prominent majority of eGFP-Dpp accumulation was observed along the basolateral cell surface of morphotrap clones.
source: However, the prominent majority of eGFP-Dpp accumulation was observed along the basolateral cell surface of morphotrap clones (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 5E.

claim: Only low amounts of eGFP-Dpp disperse in the apical/luminal compartment while the majority of eGFP-Dpp dispersal takes place along the basolateral compartment.
source: These results suggest that only low amounts of eGFP-Dpp disperse in the apical/luminal compartment while the majority of eGFP-Dpp dispersal takes place along the basolateral compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the morphotrap clone experiments.

claim: Posterior expression of morphotrap resulted in immobilization of eGFP-Dpp predominantly along the basolateral compartment of target cells adjacent to the Dpp source.
source: Posterior morphotrap expression resulted in immobilization of eGFP-Dpp predominantly along the basolateral compartment of target cells adjacent to the Dpp source.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the effects of posterior morphotrap expression.

claim: In few cases, eGFP-Dpp immobilization was observed along the apical surface of morphotrap expressing cells.
source: In few cases, eGFP-Dpp immobilization was observed along the apical surface of morphotrap expressing cells (see Figure 6B, arrow in right image and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PPE cells covering the Dpp DP source showed substantial immobilized eGFP-Dpp on their luminal surface.
source: Interestingly, PPE cells covering the Dpp DP source showed substantial immobilized eGFP-Dpp on their luminal surface (Figure 6B, asterisk in right image).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: A fraction of Dpp is secreted into the lumen and disperses in the luminal cavity.
source: This observation suggests that a fraction of Dpp is secreted into the lumen and disperses in the luminal cavity.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the observation of eGFP-Dpp on PPE cells.

claim: Posterior expression of morphotrap reduces spreading of apical and basolateral Dpp pools into the posterior compartment.
source: These results show that posterior expression of morphotrap reduces spreading of apical and basolateral Dpp pools into the posterior compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Posterior expression of GrabFP-BExt resulted in the exclusive basolateral immobilization of eGFP-Dpp close to the source.
source: Posterior expression of GrabFP-BExt resulted in the exclusive basolateral immobilization of eGFP-Dpp close to the source (Figure 6C), consistent with its restricted localization to the basolateral membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Posterior expression of GrabFP-AExt resulted in strong apical and peripodial, but also basolateral immobilization of eGFP-Dpp.
source: In sharp contrast, posterior expression of GrabFP-AExt resulted in strong apical and peripodial, but also basolateral immobilization of eGFP-Dpp (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The relative small portion of GrabFP-AExt localizing to the basolateral side is large enough to interfere with basolateral eGFP-Dpp dispersal.
source: Therefore, it seems that the relative small portion of GrabFP-AExt localizing to the basolateral side is large enough to interfere with basolateral eGFP-Dpp dispersal (or that eGFP-Dpp relocalizes GrabFP-AExt).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the observation.

claim: The increased levels of apical eGFP-Dpp immobilization might hint toward mislocalization of basolateral immobilized eGFP-Dpp to the apical compartment by GrabFP-AExt.
source: The increased levels of apical eGFP-Dpp immobilization might also hint toward mislocalization of basolateral immobilized eGFP-Dpp to the apical compartment by GrabFP-AExt.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The GrabFPExt system can be used to interfere with both apical and basolateral dispersal (morphotrap) or to specifically interfere with basolateral eGFP-Dpp dispersal (GrabFP-BExt).
source: In summary, the GrabFPExt system can be used to interfere with both apical and basolateral dispersal (morphotrap) or to specifically interfere with basolateral eGFP-Dpp dispersal (GrabFP-BExt).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the findings.

claim: Localization of GrabFP-AExt is not specific enough to exclusively interfere with apical Dpp dispersal.
source: However, localization of GrabFP-AExt is not specific enough to exclusively interfere with apical Dpp dispersal (see also Discussion).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a limitation of GrabFP-AExt.

claim: Dpp dispersal is important for wing disc growth and patterning.
source: In an earlier study using morphotrap, we reported that Dpp dispersal is important for wing disc growth and patterning (Harmansa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Harmansa et al., 2015.

claim: Dpp is prominently found in the basolateral compartment.
source: Since we find that Dpp is prominently found in the basolateral compartment, we used the newly generated GrabFP system to investigate whether basolateral Dpp dispersal is required for patterning of the wing.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a finding from the study.

claim: In control conditions (normal Dpp spreading), p-Mad forms a wide bilateral concentration gradient into the anterior and posterior compartments (>40 µm).
source: In control conditions (normal Dpp spreading), p-Mad forms a wide bilateral concentration gradient into the anterior and posterior compartments (>40 µm; see Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: Reduction of apical and basolateral spreading by expression of morphotrap in the posterior compartment resulted in a drastic reduction of the posterior p-Mad range to ~3 cells or ~10 µm.
source: In contrast, reduction of apical and basolateral spreading by expression of morphotrap in the posterior compartment resulted in a drastic reduction of the posterior p-Mad range to ~3 cells or ~10 µm (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 7B–D.

claim: Specifically interfering with basolateral Dpp spreading by posterior expression of GrabFP-BExt resulted in a reduction of posterior p-Mad range to ~3 cells or ~10 µm.
source: Interestingly, specifically interfering with basolateral Dpp spreading by posterior expression of GrabFP-BExt also resulted in a reduction of posterior p-Mad range to ~3 cells or ~10 µm (Figure 7F–H), a result strikingly similar to the morphotrap experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 7F–H.

claim: Basolateral Dpp spreading is required for proper Dpp signaling range and patterning.
source: Hence, these experiments demonstrated that basolateral Dpp spreading is required for proper Dpp signaling range and patterning and that apical/luminal Dpp spreading is not sufficient.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Apical/luminal Dpp spreading is not sufficient for proper Dpp signaling range and patterning.
source: Hence, these experiments demonstrated that basolateral Dpp spreading is required for proper Dpp signaling range and patterning and that apical/luminal Dpp spreading is not sufficient.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: The posterior wing pouch area was reduced to a similar extend when expressing either morphotrap or GrabFP-BExt in the posterior compartment.
source: We also investigated whether growth of the wing disc requires basolateral Dpp spreading. Indeed, we found that the posterior wing pouch area visualized by immunostaining against Distal-less (Dll) was reduced to a similar extend when expressing either morphotrap or GrabFP-BExt in the posterior compartment (Figure 7I–L).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 7I–L.

claim: The posterior wing blade area was reduced to a similar extend in both the morphotrap and the GrabFP-BExt conditions.
source: Accordingly, the posterior wing blade area was reduced to a similar extend in both the morphotrap and the GrabFP-BExt conditions (Figure 7M–P).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 7M–P.

claim: The distal portion of wing vein 5 was lost upon posterior expression of morphotrap or GrabFP-BExt.
source: In addition, and consistent with the strongly reduced p-Mad range, the distal portion of wing vein 5 was lost upon posterior expression of morphotrap or GrabFP-BExt (19/19 wings).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the patterning defects.

claim: Basolateral, not apical/luminal Dpp dispersal is important for patterning and size control of the wing disc and the adult wing.
source: In summary, these results show that basolateral, not apical/luminal Dpp dispersal is important for patterning and size control of the wing disc and the adult wing.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the findings.

claim: Expression of morphotrap in PPE cells to hinder luminal Dpp dispersal resulted in only very mild effects on wing patterning and growth.
source: To further test the requirement of luminal Dpp spreading, we expressed morphotrap in PPE cells to hinder luminal Dpp dispersal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). However, we observed only very mild effects on wing patterning and growth in this condition, supporting the view that apical Dpp spreading plays a minor role in wing development.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Apical Dpp spreading plays a minor role in wing development.
source: To further test the requirement of luminal Dpp spreading, we expressed morphotrap in PPE cells to hinder luminal Dpp dispersal (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). However, we observed only very mild effects on wing patterning and growth in this condition, supporting the view that apical Dpp spreading plays a minor role in wing development.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the PPE morphotrap experiments.

claim: The basolateral compartment consists of the lateral region, where epithelial cells are compactly surrounded by their neighbors, and the basal region, where cells contact the extracellular matrix (ECM) of the basal lamina (BL).
source: The basolateral compartment consists of the lateral region, where epithelial cells are compactly surrounded by their neighbors, and the basal region, where cells contact the extracellular matrix (ECM) of the basal lamina (BL).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the structure of the basolateral compartment.

claim: Dpp is known to interact with the heparin sulphate proteoglycans Dally and Dally-like localizing to the apical and lateral region.
source: Dpp is known to interact with the heparin sulphate proteoglycans Dally and Dally-like localizing to the apical and lateral region (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) as well as with Collagen IV localizing to the BL (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figures and citation to Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Dpp is known to interact with Collagen IV localizing to the BL.
source: Dpp is known to interact with the heparin sulphate proteoglycans Dally and Dally-like localizing to the apical and lateral region (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) as well as with Collagen IV localizing to the BL (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Wang et al., 2008.

claim: GrabFP-ECM is a fusion protein consisting of the coding sequence of the Drosophila Collagen IV gene viking (vkg), vhhGFP4 and mCherry inserted between the first and the second exon of vkg.
source: GrabFP-ECM is a fusion protein consisting of the coding sequence of the Drosophila Collagen IV gene viking (vkg, Yasothornsrikul et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2008), vhhGFP4 and mCherry inserted between the first and the second exon of vkg (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Yasothornsrikul et al., 1997 and Wang et al., 2008.

claim: When expressed in the larval fat body, GrabFP-ECM integrated into the BL of the wing disc.
source: When expressed in the larval fat body (r4::Gal4) GrabFP-ECM integrated into the BL of the wing disc (Figure 8A–B) as observed for wild-type collagen IV (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 8A–B and citation to Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011.

claim: When GrabFP-ECM was expressed in the fat body of dppd8/d12 mutant larvae rescued with eGFP-Dpp, high levels of eGFP-Dpp were immobilized in the BL underlying the Dpp source and low, graded levels were immobilized in the BL further away from the source stripe.
source: When GrabFP-ECM was expressed in the fat body of dppd8/d12 mutant larvae rescued with eGFP-Dpp (GrabFP-ECMRescue flies), high levels of eGFP-Dpp were immobilized in the BL underlying the Dpp source and low, graded levels were immobilized in the BL further away from the source stripe (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 8C–D.

claim: GrabFP-ECM can specifically trap Dpp and affect its dispersal in the BL, while Dpp dispersal in the lateral plane of the disc epithelium remains unaffected.
source: Hence, GrabFP-ECM can specifically trap Dpp and affect its dispersal in the BL, while Dpp dispersal in the lateral plane of the disc epithelium remains unaffected (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 8D.

claim: Wing discs of GrabFP-ECMRescue flies showed a clear reduction in p-Mad range and peak levels.
source: To study the function of Dpp dispersal in the BL, we compared p-Mad profiles in control discs and in discs of GrabFP-ECMRescue flies (Figure 8E–G). Wing discs of GrabFP-ECMRescue flies showed a clear reduction in p-Mad range and peak levels (Figure 8E–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 8E–G.

claim: The reduction in p-Mad range was accompanied by a significant reduction in wing disc pouch size.
source: The reduction in p-Mad range was accompanied by a significant reduction in wing disc pouch size (Figure 8H–J) and adult wing blade area (Figure 8K–M).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 8H–J.

claim: The reduction in p-Mad range was accompanied by a significant reduction in adult wing blade area.
source: The reduction in p-Mad range was accompanied by a significant reduction in wing disc pouch size (Figure 8H–J) and adult wing blade area (Figure 8K–M).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 8K–M.

claim: Basally secreted Dpp and/or Dpp spreading in the BL contribute to proper Dpp signaling range and size control.
source: These findings suggest that basally secreted Dpp and/or Dpp spreading in the BL contribute to proper Dpp signaling range and size control.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the GrabFP-ECM experiments.

claim: Despite a clear reduction in size, the overall patterning of the wing seemed unaffected in the GrabFP-ECM condition.
source: However, despite a clear reduction in size, the overall patterning of the wing seemed unaffected in the GrabFP-ECM condition (Figure 8L–M) suggesting that basal Dpp is not strictly required for patterning the fly wing.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 8L–M.

claim: Basal Dpp is not strictly required for patterning the fly wing.
source: However, despite a clear reduction in size, the overall patterning of the wing seemed unaffected in the GrabFP-ECM condition (Figure 8L–M) suggesting that basal Dpp is not strictly required for patterning the fly wing.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the observation.

claim: The medial region adjacent to the Dpp source is most susceptible to a reduction of Dpp signaling levels.
source: Yet, quantification of the intervein areas showed that the medial region adjacent to the Dpp source is most susceptible to a reduction of Dpp signaling levels (Figure 8N).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 8N.
